questions.problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})-3{y}^{3}$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\sqrt{\pi },2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(\sqrt{\pi },2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})-3{y}^{3})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})-3{y}^{3})\,j \\  & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2})\,i-9{y}^{2}\,j \\ ∇\,f(\sqrt{\pi },2) & =-2\sqrt{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡((\sqrt{\pi })^{2})i-9(2)^{2}\,j \\  & =-2\sqrt{\pi }\cdot 0\,i-36\,j \\  & =-36\,j \\  & =⟨0,-36⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(\sqrt{\pi },2)\cdot ⟨x-\sqrt{\pi },\,y-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨0,-36⟩\cdot ⟨x-\sqrt{\pi },\,y-2⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$

$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+2x{y}^{2}-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+2x{y}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =(6x+2{y}^{2})\text{ }i+(4xy-1)\text{ }j \\ ∇\,f(-1,1) & =(6(-1)+2(1)^{2})\,i+(4(-1)(1)-1)\,j \\  & =-4\,i-5\,j \\  & =⟨-4,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(-1,1)\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨-4,-5⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-1⟩ & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-y))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-y))\,j \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}-y)\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}-y)\,j \\ ∇f(0,\pi ) & =2(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{2}-\pi )\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{2}-\pi )\,j \\  & =0\,i+j \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $(x-y)^{2}=2x-y.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(2,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-y)^{2} & =2x-y \\ (x-y)^{2}-2x+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=(x-y)^{2}-2x+y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,0)={f}_{y}(2,0)i-{f}_{x}(2,0)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-y)^{2}-2x+y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-y)^{2}-2x+y)j \\  & =(-2(x-y)+1)i-(2(x-y)-2)j \\ t(2,0) & =(-2((2)-(0))+1)\,i-((2((2)-(0))-2)\,j \\  & =-3\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-3\,i-2\,j.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,1)={f}_{y}(1,1)i-{f}_{x}(1,1)j
$$

 

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{\pi }{2} \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(\frac{\pi }{2},0)={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},0)i-{f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{2},0)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)j \\  & =(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)j \\ t(\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =(-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡0+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡0+0\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))j \\  & =i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $i-j.$

questions.problem: At which point on the curve $x{y}^{2}=3-2y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2} & =3-2y \\ x{y}^{2}+2y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}+2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+2y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+2y)\,j \\  & =(2xy+2)\,i-{y}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i,$ we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2xy+2)\,i-{y}^{2}\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2xy+2 & =0 \\ xy+1 & =0 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-\frac{1}{x}$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2} & =3-2y \\ x{(-\frac{1}{x})}^{2} & =3-2(-\frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{1}{x} & =3+\frac{2}{x} \\ \frac{1}{x} & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $x=-\frac{1}{3},$ we get $y=3,$ and the corresponding point is $(-\frac{1}{3},3).$

questions.problem: At which point on the curve ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=xy$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =xy \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy)\,j \\  & =(-2y-x)\,i-(2x-y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i,$ we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((-2y-x)\,i-(2x-y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ -2y-x & =0 \\ x & =-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-2y$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =xy \\ (-2y)^{2}-{y}^{2} & =(-2y)y \\ 4{y}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =-2{y}^{2} \\ 5{y}^{2} & =0 \\ y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $y=0,$ we get $x=0,$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

questions.problem: At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}+2x=2xy+2y-2$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2x & =2xy+2y-2 \\ {y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$  

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y)j \\  & =(2y-2x-2)\,i-(2-2y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2y-2x-2)\,i-(2-2y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2y-2x-2 & =0 \\ 2(y-x-1) & =0 \\ y & =x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x+1$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y & =-2 \\ (x+1)^{2}+2x-2x(x+1)-2(x+1)+2 & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1)-2(x+1)+2(x+1) & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1)-\cancel{2(x+1)}+\cancel{2(x+1)} & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1) & =0 \\ (x+1)(x+1-2x) & =0 \\ (x+1)(-x+1) & =0 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=1$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(1,2).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=0$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,0).$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Tangent Line to a Level Curve
canonical_examples.problem: Given the function $f(x,y) = 6x^2+2y^2 - 2xy^2,$ find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (3,3).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y) = k$ at the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be expressed as

$$
\nabla f(x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0 \rangle  = 0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (3,3)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2x{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2x{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =(12x-2{y}^{2})\text{ }i+(4y-4xy)\text{ }j \\ ∇\,f(3,3) & =(12(3)-2(3)^{2})i+(4(3)-4(3)(3))j \\  & =18\,i-24\,j \\  & =⟨18,-24⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent to the level curve that passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)=(3,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(3,3)\cdot ⟨x-3,\,y-3⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨18,-24⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,\,y-3⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can leave our answer in this form. Or, if we want to leave our final answer in Cartesian form, we expand the dot product and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}18(x-3)-24(y-3) & =0 \\ 18x-24y+18 & =0 \\ 3x-4y+3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding a Tangent Vector to a Plane Curve
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the plane curve $x^2-3xy+4y=2.$ Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(1,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y) = x^2-3xy+4y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=2.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf t(1,1) = f_y(1,1) \ \mathbf i - f_x(1,1) \ \mathbf j
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3xy+4y)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3xy+4y)\text{ }j \\  & =(-3x+4)\text{ }i-(2x-3y)\text{ }j \\ t(1,1) & =(-3(1)+4)\text{ }i-(2(1)-3(1))\text{ }j \\  & =1\,i-(-1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $\mathbf i +\mathbf j,$ as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14151942/assets/0114bf524d085402bd27178d687a5faf176b7147c8e8726b84042b17823b6b0b.png)

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Points on a Curve at which the Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to a Given Vector
canonical_examples.problem: At which points on the curve $6xy+3y^2 =7+ y - 3x^2$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{j}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy+3{y}^{2} & =7+y-3{x}^{2} \\ 6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2} & =7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = 6xy+3y^2 - y + 3x^2 ,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=7.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf t(x,y) = f_y(x,y) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x,y) \ \mathbf j
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf t(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2})\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2})\,j \\  & =(6x+6y-1)\,i-(6y+6x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $\mathbf{j},$ we must have $\mathbf t \cdot \mathbf j = 0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((6x+6y-1)\,i-(6y+6x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -6y-6x & =0 \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-x$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy+3{y}^{2} & =7+y-3{x}^{2} \\ 6x(-x)+3(-x)^{2} & =7+(-x)-3{x}^{2} \\ -6{x}^{2}+3{x}^{2} & =7-x-3{x}^{2} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, if $x=7,$ we get $y=-7$ and the corresponding point is $(7,-7).$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to find the equation of the **tangent line** to the ellipse 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} =1
$$

 at the point $P(3,1).$

To solve this problem, we could find the slope of the line using techniques from single-variable calculus. However, we can also solve the problem by computing the gradient of a two-variable function.

Let's start by defining 

$$
f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac {y^2}{4}.
$$

Then, the given ellipse is the level curve  $f(x,y)=1.$

Now, we know that $\nabla \! f(3,1)$ is a vector that's normal to the level curve $f(x,y)= 1$ at $P(3,1).$ So, it's also normal to the tangent line to our ellipse at $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14151942/assets/3dc75e8fd4083af1bf90f46b2e875d5d552bffdc5c1cfaeabebef70f79f00828.png)

Suppose that $(x,y)$ is any point on that tangent line. Then $\mathbf v=\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle$ is a vector that's parallel to the tangent line. So $\mathbf v$ must be also orthogonal to $\nabla f(3,1),$ and since the dot product of two orthogonal vectors is zero, we have that

$$
\nabla f(3,1)\,\cdot \,\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle = 0.
$$

Now, computing $\nabla\! f$ and evaluating it at the point $P(3,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{x}{6},\frac{y}{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,f(3,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the equation of our tangent, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(3,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}(x-3)+\frac{1}{2}(y-1) & =0 \\ (x-3)+(y-1) & =0 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Tangent Line to a Level Curve
tutorials.problem:
Now, let's state the previous result more generally.

Let $f(x,y)$ be a function that's continuously differentiable at the point $P(x_0,y_0).$   If  $\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ is not the zero vector, then it is orthogonal to the tangent line to the level curve 

$$
f(x,y)= f(x_0,y_0)
$$

at the point $P.$ The equation of the tangent can then be written as

$$
\nabla\! f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0,y-y_0\rangle  = 0.
$$

Writing this explicitly, we get

$$
f_x(x_0,y_0)(x-x_0) + f_y(x_0,y_0)(y-y_0)   = 0.
$$

tutorials.name: The Tangent Vector to a Plane Curve
tutorials.problem:
Given a level curve $f(x,y) = f(x_0,y_0),$ a **tangent vector** is

$$
\mathbf t(x_0,y_0) = f_y(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf j.
$$

 

To understand why the above vector is tangent to the level curve, first recall that the gradient vector $\nabla f(x_0,y_0)$ is normal to the level curve. Now, by computing the dot product, we see that the vector $\mathbf t$ is orthogonal to the gradient vector $\nabla\! f{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f\cdot t & =({f}_{x}\text{ }i+{f}_{y}\text{ }j)\cdot ({f}_{y}\text{ }i-{f}_{x}j) \\  & ={f}_{x}{f}_{y}-{f}_{y}{f}_{x} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $\mathbf t$ is tangent to the level curve.
